extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy and the history of science; readers of Bacon's Novum Organum (assumes acquaintance with history of philosophical speculation and outlines of logic)
extracted.subtask_description: Scholarly introduction and editorial guidance for an edition of Francis Bacon's Novum Organum: explains the work's object, relation to Bacon's other writings, composition history, recommended arrangement of introductory sections, and critical judgments about particular parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thoroughness over brevity
rubrics_metrics.description: I must warn the reader that I have studied thoroughness of treatment even at the expense of occasional prolixity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editor prioritizes complete and careful treatment of special questions connected with the Novum Organum, even if that leads to long sections; this is justified as contributing to the literature and serving as the best introduction to the edition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumed reader background
rubrics_metrics.description: I have assumed in my readers a certain amount of acquaintance with the history of philosophical speculation, as well as with the outlines of logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The edition is intended for readers already familiar with philosophical history and basic logic; readers without this background may not benefit from such an edition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrangement of introductory sections
rubrics_metrics.description: Keeping apart as far as possible the expository sections from those which are mainly historical, and bringing together those which stand in any close connexion, to adopt the following order: (then enumerates §§1–17).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial ordering should separate exposition and history and group closely related topics together; follow the listed sequence of sections (dates, object, relation to other works, Latin composition question, philosophical opinions, scientific attainments, religious opinions, meaning of 'Form', method of exclusions, rejection of final causes, causes of Aristotle's failure, reaction against Aristotle, anticipations, influence, present value, opponents, bibliography).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include preliminary pieces and front-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Preliminary Pieces (Prefaces to the Instauratio Magna AND Novum Organum, Distributio Operis, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A scholarly edition should include the preliminary material (dedications, prefaces, Distributio Operis, Parasceue, Catalogus, etc.) that frame Bacon's project and guide readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide short summaries for Books I and II
rubrics_metrics.description: Short summaries of the contents of Books I and II are prefixed to those Books respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preface each book with concise summaries to orient the reader before the full text and commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include chronology (dates of events and publications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dates of the leading events in Bacon's life, and of the first publication of his principal writings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a chronological table of Bacon's life-events and publication history as essential reference material for the edition.

rubrics_metrics.name: State the object of the Novum Organum
rubrics_metrics.description: The object of the Novum Organum, and of Bacon's philosophy in general, is, stated summarily, to enlarge the dominion of man, 'Regnum Hominis', by increasing his knowledge of Nature and his power over her operations; by freeing the mind from its false prejudices and bringing it face to face with the facts of Nature; and by supplying a new, more scientific method of Induction which selects instances on certain rational principles, draws legitimate inferences, and thus guarantees the truth of first principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expositions and commentary should present Bacon's goal as practical mastery of nature through a disciplined induction that avoids authority-driven error and grounds deductive reasoning in justified first principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book I's preliminary task
rubrics_metrics.description: Previously to laying down any rules for [the new method] or exemplifying its employment, it is necessary to insist on its importance, to free the mind from those obstacles which might prevent it from having recourse to this assistance, to point out the sources of our errors in the past, and to shew what hopes may be conceived of the future. The preliminary task is undertaken in Book I.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Book I should focus on diagnosing intellectual obstacles (idola), explaining the importance of a new method, and clearing the conceptual ground before formal rules are given in Book II.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book II as formal exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: The formal exposition of the method begins in Book II, but the work, as left by Bacon, is not completed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat Book II as where Bacon sets out the systematic rules of induction; note incompleteness and missing parts when evaluating his method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness / fragmentary status
rubrics_metrics.description: The Novum Organum is only a fragment of the much larger work which Bacon contemplated under that title; the enumeration of the parts wanting will be found in Book II, Aph. 21, and again in Aph. 52.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars and editors must acknowledge the incomplete nature of Bacon's plan and point readers to aphorisms that enumerate intended but missing material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful drafting and textual history
rubrics_metrics.description: The Novum Organum, and especially the first Book, is the most carefully written of all Bacon's philosophical works. According to Rawley, it was written out twelve several times, and we have just seen by what a number of essays the final effort was preceded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textual apparatus should document multiple drafts, manuscript corrections, and stages of composition; stress meticulous revision as a criterion of authorial care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third part (Phaenomena Universi) requirement: arranged and sifted materials
rubrics_metrics.description: The Third Part of the Great Instauration... was to contain a collection of arranged and sifted materials on which the method of induction was to work. In the Historia Naturalis Bacon published a small instalment and aditus to proposed treatises; 'in the Historia Naturali bona, et bene instituta, claves sunt et Scientiarum et Operum.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An adequate execution of Bacon's method requires carefully collected, arranged, and sifted empirical materials (histories) to serve as the basis for induction; editions should identify and present these materials (Historia Ventorum, Historia Vitae et Mortis, Sylva Sylvarum, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate Sylva Sylvarum critically
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sylva Sylvarum... is the least creditable of Bacon's philosophical works, and has furnished Liebig and other antagonists with many of their most effective weapons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat Sylva Sylvarum with caution as an unreliable or problematic source in places; note Rawley's editorial role and criticisms from later scientists when using its observations as evidence of Bacon's method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret New Atlantis as programmatic vision
rubrics_metrics.description: The New Atlantis... bears the stamp of his genius... and... is credited... with having, to a large extent, suggested the foundation and programme of our own Royal Society. The story of Solomon's House is nothing more than a vision of the practical results which he anticipated from the study of natural history diligently and systematically carried on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read the New Atlantis as Bacon's imaginative sketch of the practical institutional outcome of his method; use it to illuminate his aims for organized scientific practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical method: example-based exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: The plan [of setting forth his meaning mainly by means of an example] is worked out in the second book of the Novum Organum. The example first selected by Bacon was Motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bacon often illustrates his method by a detailed worked example (e.g., the inquiry into Motion); editors/commentators should highlight these exemplars as central to understanding his procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for attributing Latin authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Positive evidence that the Novum Organum was written in Latin by Bacon: Archbishop Tenison's statement; Hume's remark that most of Bacon's performances were composed in Latin; Bacon's manuscripts (Cogitata et Visa) corrected throughout in his own handwriting; Bacon's commonplace book entries in English and Latin; the Latin of the First Book bears the mark of Bacon's genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing whether Bacon wrote the Latin texts himself, weigh documentary testimony (Tenison, Hume), autographic corrections, bilingual manuscript practice, and stylistic fingerprinting rather than speculative claims of translators' involvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare Novum Organum with related drafts and fragments
rubrics_metrics.description: Portions of Valerius Terminus, Partis Secundae Delineatio, Cogitata et Visa, Temporis Partus Masculus, Filum Labyrinthi, and other fragments cover similar ground and may profitably be compared with the Novum Organum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars should systematically compare the Novum Organum with its preparatory drafts and related tracts to trace development of ideas, repetitions, and editorial decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include Catalogus/Desiderata (specific materials for induction)
rubrics_metrics.description: The volume is closed by a Catalogus Historiarum Particularium Secundum Capita, or list of desiderata in the specific materials for induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editions and studies should present Bacon's catalogue of desired natural histories as a research agenda and a guide to the empirical materials necessary for inductive work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of Bacon's philosophical status and influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Bacon was not the founder of a philosophical school... though not the founder of any special school of philosophy, it seems... that his exposition of his method, and, perhaps, also individual expressions in his writings, contributed in no small degree to the creation of what is commonly called the empirical tradition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating Bacon's originality and influence, avoid labeling him as the founder of a sect; instead assess his contribution in promoting empirical methods and shaping later scientific practice.
